title: Loops
summary: A **loop** runs a block of code repeatedly until a condition stops it, so you can process lists, repeat actions, and automate work without copying the same statements over and over.

subtopics.title: The for loop
subtopics.explanation: The classic for loop bundles three parts in one line: an initializer that runs once, a condition checked before every pass, and an update that runs after each pass. It is the go-to loop when you know how many times to repeat or need the index. Because all three parts are explicit, it is easy to read and easy to control.

subtopics.title: while and do-while
subtopics.explanation: A while loop checks its condition before each pass, so it may run zero times if the condition starts false. A do-while loop runs the body once first and checks the condition afterwards, so it always runs at least once. Use while when you loop until some event happens rather than a fixed count.

subtopics.title: for...of — iterating values
subtopics.explanation: for...of walks through the values of any iterable — arrays, strings, Maps, Sets — without needing an index. It is the cleanest way to read each element when you do not care about position. It does not work directly on plain objects because plain objects are not iterable.
subtopics.example:
for (const ch of 'hi') { console.log(ch); } // 'h', 'i'
for (const x of [10, 20]) { console.log(x); } // 10, 20

subtopics.title: for...in — iterating keys
subtopics.explanation: for...in loops over the enumerable property names (keys) of an object. It is meant for objects, not arrays, because it yields keys as strings and can include inherited properties. For arrays prefer for...of or a normal for loop to get values and reliable order.

subtopics.title: break and continue
subtopics.explanation: break exits the entire loop immediately, skipping any remaining passes. continue skips only the rest of the current pass and jumps to the next one. They let you short-circuit work — stop once you find a match, or ignore items that do not qualify — without awkward extra flags.

subtopics.title: Looping arrays vs objects
subtopics.explanation: Arrays are ordered lists, so iterate their values with for...of or forEach. Objects are unordered key/value bags, so iterate them with for...in or by extracting Object.keys/values/entries. Mixing them up — using for...in on an array or for...of on a plain object — is a frequent beginner bug.
subtopics.example:
for (const v of [1, 2]) {}            // array values
for (const [k, v] of Object.entries({a:1})) {} // object pairs

subtopics.title: forEach vs for
subtopics.explanation: Array.forEach runs a callback for each element and reads cleanly, but you cannot break out of it early and it ignores return values. A plain for or for...of loop lets you break, continue, and use await naturally. Pick forEach for simple side effects, and a real loop when you need control flow.
subtopics.example:
[1, 2, 3].forEach((x) => console.log(x));
// cannot break out of forEach early

subtopics.title: Infinite loops and labelled loops
subtopics.explanation: An infinite loop never satisfies its exit condition (forgetting to update the counter is the usual cause) and freezes the page, so always make sure the condition can become false. Labelled loops let break/continue target an outer loop from inside a nested one, which is handy for grid or matrix scans.

foundations.overview: Loops are the core tool for repetition in JavaScript. Instead of writing the same statement many times, you write it once inside a loop and let the engine repeat it while a condition holds. The main flavours are for, while, do-while, for...of, and for...in, plus break and continue for fine control.
foundations.formalDefinition: A loop is a control-flow construct that repeatedly executes a block of statements, evaluating a controlling condition before (or after) each iteration to decide whether to continue or stop.
foundations.whyItMatters: Almost every real program processes collections — rendering lists, summing values, validating inputs, polling for changes. Loops are how you express 'do this for each item' or 'keep going until done', making them one of the first essential building blocks of programming.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a loop as a worker on an assembly line. The condition is the supervisor asking 'is there more to do?'; while the answer is yes, the worker runs the body once more, then checks again. break is the worker leaving the line; continue is skipping the current item and grabbing the next.
foundations.browserPerspective: JavaScript runs on a single thread, so a long-running or infinite loop blocks the main thread: the page cannot paint, scroll, or respond to clicks until the loop finishes. That is why tight loops over huge data sets can freeze the UI and why the browser may warn about an unresponsive script.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Building HTML for a list of products, summing items in a cart, searching an array for a match, retrying a request until it succeeds, and stepping through characters of a string are all everyday loop tasks.
foundations.businessImpact: Correct, efficient loops keep interfaces responsive and data accurate; a bug like an off-by-one error or an accidental infinite loop can corrupt results or freeze the app, directly hurting users.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Choosing the right loop (for index control, for...of for values, for...in for keys) makes code clearer and less bug-prone, and understanding break/continue avoids tangled boolean flags.
foundations.performanceImpact: Loop choice and body cost dominate hot paths. Doing expensive work (DOM updates, allocations) inside a loop instead of batching it is a top cause of jank; minimizing work per iteration keeps loops fast.
commonUseCases: Iterating an array to render or transform each item
Summing, counting, or searching through a collection
Repeating an action a fixed number of times
Reading object key/value pairs to build output

commonMisconceptions.myth: for...in is the way to loop over arrays.
commonMisconceptions.reality: for...in iterates keys as strings and can include inherited properties; for arrays use for...of, forEach, or a plain for loop to get values in order.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You can break out of forEach with break or return.
commonMisconceptions.reality: break is a syntax error in forEach and return only ends the current callback; to stop early, use a for/for...of loop or methods like some/find.

config.intro: Follow `for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++)` as it counts from 0 to 2 and then stops.

steps.name: Initialize
steps.detail: The initializer `let i = 0` runs exactly once, before the loop body.

steps.name: Check condition
steps.detail: The condition `i < 3` is evaluated. If true, the body runs; if false, the loop ends.

steps.name: Run the body
steps.detail: The statements inside { } execute for the current value of i.

steps.name: Update
steps.detail: The update `i++` runs after the body, increasing i by 1.

steps.name: Re-check and repeat
steps.detail: Control returns to the condition; this repeats until `i < 3` becomes false.

steps.name: Exit
steps.detail: When i reaches 3 the condition is false, so the loop stops and code after it runs.

codeLab.title: Sum the numbers in an array
codeLab.instructions: Write a loop that adds up every number in the `nums` array and stores the result in `total`. Use any loop you like, then log the total.
hints: Start total at 0 before the loop.
Use for...of to read each value, then add it to total with +=.

debuggingLab.title: The accidental infinite loop
debuggingLab.symptom: The page freezes and never logs 'done' — the loop runs forever.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: The condition `i < 5` never becomes false because i is never updated inside the loop. With i stuck at 0, the loop body repeats endlessly and blocks the single JavaScript thread, so 'done' is never reached.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to increment or otherwise change the loop variable.
Updating a different variable than the one in the condition.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Make the loop run exactly five times and then log 'done'.

theory.question: What is the difference between for...of and for...in?
theory.directAnswer: for...of iterates over the values of an iterable (arrays, strings, Maps, Sets), while for...in iterates over the enumerable keys of an object. Use for...of for array/string values and for...in for object property names.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two looping syntaxes: for...of yields each value; for...in yields each key as a string.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: for...in came first for object properties; for...of was added in ES6 to cleanly iterate any iterable's values without an index.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: for...of uses the object's iterator protocol; for...in walks the enumerable property names, including inherited ones, in an engine-defined order.

theory.whyImportant: Choosing the wrong one is a classic beginner bug — for...in on an array gives string indices and can include extras, while for...of on a plain object throws because objects are not iterable.
theory.realWorldExample: Use for...of to render each item in a product array, and for...in (or Object.entries) to display each field of a settings object.

nestedTopics.title: Iterables
nestedTopics.explanation: Arrays, strings, Maps, and Sets are iterable; plain objects are not.

nestedTopics.title: Enumerable keys
nestedTopics.explanation: for...in only sees enumerable properties, including inherited ones.

nestedTopics.title: Object.entries
nestedTopics.explanation: A safe way to loop object key/value pairs with for...of.

followUps.question: Why can for...of loop over a string but for...in cannot give its characters?
followUps.answer: Strings are iterable, so for...of yields each character; for...in would yield index keys ('0','1',...), not the characters themselves.

followUps.question: How do you loop an object's values safely?
followUps.answer: Use for...of over Object.values(obj), or for...of over Object.entries(obj) for key/value pairs.

theory.question: What is the difference between break and continue?
theory.directAnswer: break exits the loop entirely, skipping all remaining iterations, while continue skips only the rest of the current iteration and moves on to the next one. Both control flow inside loops.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two loop control statements: break stops the loop; continue short-circuits to the next pass.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: They let you express early-exit and skip logic directly instead of using extra boolean flags or nested conditionals.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: break transfers control to the statement after the loop; continue jumps to the loop's update/condition step for the next iteration.

theory.whyImportant: They make search-and-stop and filter-while-looping patterns concise, and labelled versions can target outer loops in nested code.
theory.realWorldExample: break out of a search loop the moment you find a matching user; continue to skip invalid rows while processing a dataset.

nestedTopics.title: Labelled break
nestedTopics.explanation: break outerLabel exits an outer loop from inside a nested one.

nestedTopics.title: continue in for vs while
nestedTopics.explanation: In a for loop continue still runs the update expression before re-checking.

followUps.question: Does continue in a for loop skip the i++ update?
followUps.answer: No — continue jumps to the update step, so i++ still runs before the condition is re-checked.

scenario.question: You need to stop processing a list as soon as you find the first item over a threshold. Which loop and statement would you use and why?
scenario.directAnswer: I'd use a for...of (or plain for) loop with a break: iterate the values, and the moment an item exceeds the threshold, record it and break out so I don't waste passes. I'd avoid forEach because you can't break out of it.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An early-exit search where you stop at the first match.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Once the answer is found, continuing wastes work and can be incorrect if you only want the first hit.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: A for...of loop reads each value; an if check triggers break, transferring control past the loop immediately.

scenario.whyImportant: Knowing which loops allow early exit (and that forEach does not) is a common practical interview signal.

nestedTopics.title: Array.find
nestedTopics.explanation: A built-in alternative that returns the first matching element.

nestedTopics.title: Array.some
nestedTopics.explanation: Returns true and stops once a predicate matches.

followUps.question: Could you avoid the loop entirely?
followUps.answer: Yes — Array.find returns the first matching element and short-circuits internally, which is often cleaner than a manual loop and break.

coding.question: Write a function fizzbuzz(n) that returns an array where each entry from 1 to n is 'Fizz' for multiples of 3, 'Buzz' for multiples of 5, 'FizzBuzz' for both, otherwise the number.
coding.thoughtProcess: I'll loop from 1 to n. For each number I check divisibility by 3 and 5. Order matters: check the 15 (both) case first, or build the string by appending. I'll push the result into an output array and return it.
coding.lineByLine: A for loop runs i from 1 to n. We build s by appending 'Fizz' when i is divisible by 3 and 'Buzz' when divisible by 5, so multiples of 15 become 'FizzBuzz'. If s is still empty, `s || i` falls back to the number itself, which we push to the output array.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) — one pass from 1 to n.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(n) — the output array holds n entries.

alternativeApproaches.title: Explicit if/else
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Check the i % 15 case first, then 3, then 5, then the number.

followUps.question: Why check % 3 and % 5 separately instead of % 15?
followUps.answer: Appending 'Fizz' then 'Buzz' naturally produces 'FizzBuzz' for multiples of 15, avoiding a separate branch and reducing duplication.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Loops are the building block beneath array methods and rendering layers. Many higher-level abstractions (map, filter, reduce, template rendering) are loops underneath, so understanding loops clarifies how those tools behave and where their cost comes from.
productionDeepDive.performance: The per-iteration cost and total count determine loop speed. Hoist invariant work out of the loop, avoid repeated DOM reads/writes inside it, and batch updates; a tight loop over large data on the main thread can freeze the UI.
productionDeepDive.security: Loops over user-supplied data should bound their length and validate inputs; unbounded loops driven by external input can become denial-of-service vectors that hang the thread.
productionDeepDive.scaling: For very large data sets, chunk the work across animation frames or move it to a Web Worker so the loop does not block rendering and input handling on the single main thread.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Choosing the loop that matches the data (for...of for values, for...in/Object.entries for objects) and preferring expressive array methods for simple transforms keeps loop code readable and intent-revealing.
productionDeepDive.observability: Long tasks caused by heavy loops appear in the browser's Performance panel as blocking main-thread work; the Long Tasks API can surface iterations that exceed 50ms and hurt responsiveness.

caseStudies.problem: Rendering thousands of rows in one synchronous loop froze the page.
caseStudies.solution: Virtualize the list and process rows in batches per frame instead of one giant loop.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: More complex code in exchange for a responsive UI.
caseStudies.lessons: Big synchronous loops on the main thread are a common, avoidable source of jank.

keyTakeaways: Loops repeat a block of code while a condition holds, letting you process collections and repeat work without duplication.
Use for when you need the index, while/do-while for condition-driven repetition, for...of for values, and for...in for object keys.
break exits a loop entirely; continue skips to the next iteration — both avoid clumsy boolean flags.
for...in is for objects and for...of is for iterables; mixing them up is a common beginner bug, and forEach cannot be broken out of.
Always ensure the loop condition can become false, and avoid heavy work per iteration to keep the single-threaded UI responsive.
